newsitem.title: RUSSIA: No second-class citizens in NATO, U.S. aide says.
newsitem.headline: No second-class citizens in NATO, U.S. aide says.

text.p: Any NATO concessions to Russia over the Western alliance's eastward expansion plans will not be made at the expense of new member states, a senior aide to U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Thursday.

"There are certain lines that we're not going to cross now or later (and) one of those lines is that there are not going to be second-class citizens in the alliance," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
"All the members of the alliance, whether new or old, are going to be full members of the alliance ... They are going to have all the rights of any member of the alliance."

He spoke to reporters on the way to Moscow where Albright, on her first overseas trip as secretary of state, would spell out a package of sweeteners designed to ease Russian fears about NATO'S plans to take in former Warsaw Pact states as members.

But some U.S officials are concerned that the heavy push to make Russia comfortable with expansion may unsettle prospective new NATO members who are suspicious of Moscow's long-term intentions and fear NATO may bend too far to accommodate Moscow.
Leaders of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation plan a July summit in Madrid at which they intend to issue formal invitations to the alliance's first new post-Cold War members.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic are the top contenders for membership.
Albright was to hold talks with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Thursday, and then meet President Boris Yeltsin on Friday.
Russia fiercely opposes expansion, calling it threatening. U.S. officials acknowledge this resistance is unlikely to go away soon and say all sides will just "have to deal with it".

"The challenge here is to see if, despite Russia's strong opposition to NATO enlargement, we can deepen, broaden and define what NATO-Russia cooperation will look like in the years to come," the senior official said.
Albright said in London on Wednesday the sweeteners were a conventional arms reductions proposal which NATO approved that day and a more detailed proposal for a NATO-Russia charter.
The charter proposal includes the concept of a joint military unit and vastly increased consultation between Moscow and the alliance.

In another gesture, the senior official said that while the alliance would not ban the stationing of nuclear arms in new NATO states, he could envision including in the proposed charter a reaffirmation of a declaration made by NATO last year.
That declaration says the alliance has no intention, plan or reason to change its current nuclear arms deployments.
"There certainly is no reason why that statement of NATO policy cannot be reaffirmed as part of the formal understanding or charter of some kind between NATO and Russia," he said.
But he said it would reaffirm "a unilateral NATO position" and not be subject to negotiation with Russia.
Western officials believe this commitment does not compromise the membership of new NATO states because not all existing alliance members have atomic arms on their territories.
NATO has ruled out any Russia veto over its decision-making.

Officials say the new conventional arms reduction proposal, which modifies the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe treaty, should go a long way to calming Moscow's fears that NATO could pile up weapons on Russia's borders.

The Russians want a legally-binding contract providing security guarantees. The Americans say this proposed modification of CFE, which is a treaty requiring ratification by 30 signatory states, amounts to that legally-binding document.

The proposal also establishes a "sensitive geographic region" in central Europe comprising the Baltic enclave of Kaliningrad, Ukraine, Slovakia, Belarus, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland. It makes clear that ground equipment in that area cannot increase, officials said.
